sentences.text: Fossil remains include numerous teeth, a dorsal vertebra, vertebral centra, and pelvic bones.
The skeleton also preserves parts of the fibula and tibia, along with metatarsals.
Ventral and neck osteoderms are present in the material recovered from the ground.
Unlike other members of its family, the squamosal bone of this animal is notably narrow.
The skull features a long, narrow snout and a small cranial vault.
A distinctive ridge runs along the midline of the frontal bone.
The lower jaw possesses a long symphysis where the two halves join together.
One species, S. shunanensis, had a snout that was longer than others, measuring about three times the length of the postorbital region.
The tip of the jaw in the Thai species is spoon-shaped and wider than the section immediately behind it.
Fossils from Kyrgyzstan represent the westernmost record of the animal's geographic range.
S. junggarensis is the best known species, first described in 1996 from Late Jurassic deposits in the Junggar Basin of Xinjiang, China.
Material collected from Kyrgyzstan in the 1980s was not described until 2000.
S. shunanensis was described in 2005 from Middle Jurassic rocks in Zigong, Sichuan, China.
Sunosuchus thailandicus was described from northeastern Thailand in 1980.
Up to four species have been assigned to the genus Sunosuchus.
The fauna found with Sunosuchus in Kyrgyzstan, including temnospondyl amphibians and xinjiangchelyid turtles, indicates freshwater environments.
The presence of marine hybodont sharks and dipnoans in Kyrgyzstan strata suggests the area was estuarine rather than entirely freshwater.
The regions where Sunosuchus fossils were found shared a fauna with temnospondyl amphibians and Xinjiangchelyidae turtles, indicating freshwater ecosystems.
The discovery of hybodont sharks and marine dipnoans in the same strata suggests the area was an estuary rather than a purely freshwater environment.
Sunosuchus was initially classified as a pholidosaurid due to its long, long-snouted jaws.
Despite similarities with pholidosaurs, Sunosuchus shares features that ally it with goniopholidids.
Sunosuchus belongs to the family Goniopholididae.
Sunosuchus was initially classified as a pholidosaurid because its elongated jaws made it a long-snouted crocodyliform.
Despite similarities to pholidosaurids, Sunosuchus shares several traits with goniopholidids that place it in that group.
The traits linking Sunosuchus to goniopholidids might be considered primitive features shared by both goniopholidids and pholidosaurids within Mesosuchia.
It is possible that Sunosuchus, or at least S. thailandicus, represents a pholidosaurid that retained ancient characteristics rather than being an advanced goniopholidid.
The parent group of the genus Sunosuchus is Goniopholididae.
Sunosuchus is classified in the class Reptilia.
Sunosuchus fossils date from the Middle Jurassic to the Early Cretaceous, with possible Early Jurassic occurrences.
Fossils of Sunosuchus have been found in China, Kyrgyzstan, and Thailand and are Jurassic in age, though some may be Early Cretaceous.
Sunosuchus lived from the Bajocian to the Tithonian stages, between 170.9 and 143.1 million years ago.
The fossil material found in Kyrgyzstan represents the westernmost record of Sunosuchus's geographic range.
A newly discovered specimen suggests that S. thailandicus is distinct enough to be placed in its own genus, Chalawan.
